'''''Cosmarium''''' is a large [[genus (biology)|genus]] of desmids ([[Desmidiaceae]]), a group of [[green algae]] closely related to the land plants ([[Embryophyta]]).<ref name="pmid12569426">{{cite journal |vauthors=Gontcharov AA, Marin BA, Melkonian MA |title=Molecular phylogeny of conjugating green algae (Zygnemophyceae, Streptophyta) inferred from SSU rDNA sequence comparisons |journal=J. Mol. Evol. |volume=56 |issue=1 |pages=89–104 |date=January 2003 |pmid=12569426 |doi=10.1007/s00239-002-2383-4}}</ref><ref>See the [[National Center for Biotechnology Information|NCBI]] [https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/Taxonomy/Browser/wwwtax.cgi?mode=Info&id=33100 webpage on Cosmarium].  Data extracted from the {{cite web | url=https://ftp.ncbi.nih.gov/pub/taxonomy/ | title=NCBI taxonomy resources | publisher=[[National Center for Biotechnology Information]] | access-date=2007-03-19}}</ref> Members of this genus are microscopic and found in [[freshwater]] habitats around the world.<ref name=Prescott1981/>

The name ''Cosmarium'' comes from the Greek word κοσμάριον - ''kosmarion'', meaning a small ornament.<ref name=CarolinaLucidKey>{{cite web|url=https://fmp.conncoll.edu/Silicasecchidisk/LucidKeys3.5/Keys_v3.5/Carolina35_Key/Media/Html/Cosmarium_Main.html|title=Cosmarium|first1= Hannah|last1= Shayler|first2=Peter A.|last2=Siver|work=Carolina Lucid Key to Freshwater Algae|publisher=Connecticut College | date=2004 |access-date=2024-11-28 }}</ref>

==Description==
''Cosmarium'', with few exceptions, consists of single cells and is thus microscopic. Cells are constricted in the middle, giving them a bilobed appearance;<ref>Guiry, M.D., John, D.M., Rindi, F. and McCarthy, Y.K. 2007. ''New Survey of Clare Island Volume 6: The Freshwater and Terrestrial Algae.'' Royal Irish Academy. {{ISBN|978-1-904890-31-7}}</ref> the two halves are called semicells. Cells come in a variety of different shapes. The cell wall may be smooth or ornamented with spines, granules, scrobiculations (pits), or pores. Cells are generally flattened.<ref name=Hall2014/> Cells usually have one or two [[chloroplast]]s filling the cell; each chloroplast contains [[pyrenoid]]s, typically one or two.<ref name=Prescott1981>{{cite book | isbn = 9780835737920 | title = A Synopsis of North American Desmids. Part II: Desmidiaceae: Placodermae. Section 3 | last1 = Prescott | first1 = G. W. | last2 = Croasdale | first2 = H. T. | last3 = Vinyard | first3 = W. C. | last4 = Bicudo | first4 = C. E. M. | publisher = University of Nebraska Press | location = Lincoln | date = 1981 | pages = 720 }}</ref>

===Identification===
Species identification of ''Cosmarium'' depends on the shape of the cells and their ornamentation, and can be difficult.<ref name=Hall2014>{{cite book |editor-first1=John D.|editor-last1=Wehr|editor-first2=Robert G.|editor-last2=Sheath|editor-first3=J. Patrick|editor-last3=Kociolek |date= 2014 |edition=2 |title= Freshwater Algae of North America: Ecology and Classification |last1= Hall|first1=John D.| last2=McCourt |first2=Richard M. |chapter= Chapter 9. Conjugating Green Algae Including Desmids |url= |location= |publisher= Elsevier Inc. |page= |isbn=978-0-12-385876-4 }}</ref> In addition, the genera ''[[Actinotaenium]]'' and ''[[Euastrum]]'' can be similar to various species of ''Cosmarium''. ''Actinotaenium'' is generally circular in cross section, and ''Euastrum'' usually (but not always) has a notch at the tip of each semicell.<ref name=Hall2014/>

==Taxonomy==
''Cosmarium'' is the largest genus of desmids, with over 1,000 species. It is an artificial genus: the defining characteristics of the genus are vague and arbitrary, and there are some species that are intermediate between several different genera.<ref name=Gontcharov/> For this reason, it has been called a [[wastebasket taxon]].<ref name=Teiling>{{cite journal | title=The genus ''Staurodesmus'': A taxonomic study | last1=Teiling | first1=Einar | journal=Arkiv för Botanik | volume=6 | issue=11 | pages=467–629 }}</ref> It is also not [[monophyletic]], as molecular phylogenetic studies have shown that the form of ''Cosmarium'' evolved independently many times over. Despite this, the genus is still in use, because there is no known way of classifying desmids in line with their evolutionary history.<ref name=Gontcharov>{{cite journal |last1=Gontcharov|first1=A.A.|last2=Melkonian |first2=M.| year = 2008 | title = In search of monophyletic taxa in the family Desmidiaceae (Zygnematophyceae, Viridiplantae): The genus ''Cosmarium'' | journal = [[American Journal of Botany]] | volume = 95 | issue = 9 | pages = 1079–1095 | doi = 10.3732/ajb.0800046 | pmid = 21632428| doi-access = free }}</ref>

==Habitat==
''Cosmarium'' and other desmid genera tend to prefer [[Trophic state index|oligotrophic]], somewhat acidic water habitats,<ref name=Hall2014/> but some species exist in more eutrophic and/or basic habitats. Some species, which are small and mostly plain, form a community known as a "Cosmarietum"; these may be further associated with a community of ''[[Closterium]]'' species forming a Cosmarietum-Closterietum association.<ref name=Prescott1981/>
